demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with the more trauma-disconnected pattern implied by emotionless/numb recall and sensory reliving. Those can occasionally coexist, but this combination is clinically questionable as a compact 3-item profile because one item suggests relatively integrated verbal access while the others suggest poorly integrated or detached trauma memory.

issues.item: Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' is a poor fit for the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. It implies an intruder/home-security threat that is not supported by the other selected Memory or Negative Appraisal items, which center more on guilt, identity change, and trauma recall rather than fear of break-in or assault. This makes the Threat profile less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, repeated checking of doors and windows being locked suggests a home-intrusion/interpersonal danger theme that is not supported by the other threat, memory, or appraisal items. The rest of the profile centers on guilt, altered self-view, disconnection, and poorly elaborated trauma memory rather than fear of external attack.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Loss of connection to community and culture is not impossible, but in this profile it is insufficiently linked to the stated trauma and the other selected items. The other appraisals focus on self-doubt and identity change after causing harm, whereas this item introduces a broader sociocultural rupture that is not reflected elsewhere in memory or threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette:
# Layla

Layla was thirty-one when she came to her first appointment, sitting rigidly in the waiting room chair, her phone clutched in her lap. The intake form listed her occupation as social media manager for a mid-sized marketing firm, a job she had held for four years—until six weeks ago, when she had taken what her employer called "medical leave." She wore a loose cardigan despite the warm weather, and when Dr. Morrison extended her hand in greeting, Layla flinched visibly, her whole body tensing as though bracing for impact.

The event itself had occurred eighteen months prior, on a Tuesday evening in late winter. Layla had been driving home from work on the highway, her mind half-occupied with a campaign brief she'd been reviewing, when she glanced down at her phone to silence an incoming call. The moment of inattention lasted perhaps two seconds. A cyclist had swerved into her lane without warning—or so it seemed to her in the fractured seconds that followed. She heard the impact before she felt it, a sickening thud that seemed to come from everywhere at once. The cyclist, a man in his sixties, had been thrown across her hood. His femur had shattered. He'd spent three months in the hospital, and though he had eventually recovered enough to walk with a cane, Layla had been informed of every stage of his rehabilitation through a victim services coordinator. She had not caused the accident deliberately, but she had caused it nonetheless.

In the months that followed, Layla had come to believe that she could not be trusted with the simplest decisions, let alone the responsibility of driving or managing her own life. The person she had been before—confident enough to manage social media for a company of two hundred employees, assured enough to make quick judgment calls in real time—felt like a stranger to her now. This conviction that she was fundamentally unsafe, that some essential part of her had been destroyed, seemed to pull the memory toward her unbidden; the more she told herself she should have seen the cyclist coming, the more vividly she could see his body arc across her windshield, as if her certainty of her own culpability made the moment impossible to forget. The belief that she was permanently broken fed directly into the memory itself, making it sharper and more intrusive—as if her conviction of her own danger excavated the moment from deeper inside her, pulled it closer, made it more vivid and harder to escape. Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory easier to find; it sat there waiting, proof of her failure, summoned again and again by her own certainty that she was irreparably flawed. She had permanently damaged not just a man's leg but something essential in herself. This conviction had crystallized slowly, then completely. When she tried to explain it to her ex-husband during one of their custody exchanges, the words had simply vanished. She knew what she meant, knew the weight of it, but her mouth produced only fragments: "I can't... I'm not... I don't know who I am anymore." He had stared at her, then asked if she was seeing someone. She had said no.

The intrusive memories began about three months after the accident, arriving without warning and with a sensory intensity that felt like a fresh violation. The smell came first—the particular acrid-sweet odor of burning rubber and something metallic that had filled the car immediately after impact. Weeks later, she could be sitting at her desk at work, reviewing a campaign schedule, when that smell would ghost across her nostrils with such vividness that she would have to grip the desk to orient herself to the present. Sometimes the memories came without feeling attached, as if she were watching footage of someone else's catastrophe—she could see the cyclist's body arc across the windshield, could hear her own scream, but feel nothing, numb as though observing from behind glass. Other times the memory brought such a surge of guilt and horror that she would have to excuse herself to the bathroom.

This fractured recollection of what she had done fed back into her conviction that she could not trust herself. Each time the memory surfaced, it seemed to confirm that she was fundamentally unsafe, that her judgment was irreparably compromised. And this belief—that she was now someone dangerous, someone who could hurt people—had begun to alter how her body moved through the world. The more she convinced herself that she was broken, the more readily the memory arrived, sharper and more detailed, as though her shame was excavating it from deeper and deeper inside her. She had become hypervigilant, scanning every interaction for signs of threat. At the office, she had started to interpret neutral comments from colleagues as criticism. When her supervisor asked her to review a campaign timeline, Layla had heard it as an accusation that she was incompetent. Her startle response had become pronounced; a colleague had touched her shoulder one afternoon to ask about a meeting, and Layla had jerked away so violently that she'd knocked over her coffee. On days when her vigilance was at its peak—when every neutral comment felt like a threat, when her body was already braced for danger—the intrusive memories seemed to surface more readily, pulled to the surface by the adrenaline coursing through her, fully formed and visceral. The colleague had apologized, looking confused and hurt. Layla had not explained.

What frightened her most was that these false alarms—her sense of danger when none existed—seemed to confirm her core fear: that she could no longer read situations accurately, that her perception was corrupted, that trusting herself to navigate even ordinary moments was a risk to everyone around her. When she received an unexpected text message, her heart would race as though she were about to be confronted. When she heard a siren in the distance, she would feel certain it was coming for her. On nights when the threat felt highest, when she lay awake convinced that some consequence of her negligence was about to arrive, the memory would surface in the dark—vivid, unbidden, as if her hypervigilance had dragged it to the surface to remind her of what she had done. But it was not only the vigilance itself that pulled the memory forward; it was the underlying conviction that she deserved this punishment, that she was fundamentally dangerous, that fed the memory its intensity and made it impossible to release. The stronger her belief that she was broken, the more the memory seemed to confirm it, arriving fully formed and sensory-rich, as if her shame was calling it up from within her. Her ex-husband had begun to notice her anxiety during their exchanges; she would flinch when he approached, and he had asked, with genuine concern, whether something else had happened. She could not tell him that she was afraid of herself.

By the time she arrived at the clinic, Layla had withdrawn almost entirely from her job. She had told her supervisor that she needed time off, but the truth was more complicated: she was afraid that her impaired judgment would hurt someone again, that she would miss something crucial in a campaign brief and cause some unforeseen harm. It was easier to stay home, to limit her contact with others, to try to make herself small and harmless. She was hoping that therapy might somehow restore her to who she had been, or at least help her understand why she had become someone she no longer recognized.

When her supervisor asked her to review a campaign timeline, Layla had heard it as an accusation that she was incompetent. Her startle response had become pronounced; a colleague had touched her shoulder one afternoon to ask about a meeting, and Layla had jerked away so violently that she'd knocked over her coffee. On days when her vigilance was at its peak—when every neutral comment felt like a threat, when her body was already braced for danger—the intrusive memories seemed to surface more readily, pulled to the surface by the adrenaline coursing through her, fully formed and visceral. The colleague had apologized, looking confused and hurt. Layla had not explained.

What frightened her most was that these false alarms—her sense of danger when none existed—seemed to confirm her core fear: that she could no longer read situations accurately, that her perception was corrupted, that trusting herself to navigate even ordinary moments was a risk to everyone around her. When she received an unexpected text message, her heart would race as though she were about to be confronted. When she heard a siren in the distance, she would feel certain it was coming for her. On nights when the threat felt highest, when she lay awake convinced that some consequence of her negligence was about to arrive, the memory would surface in the dark—vivid, unbidden, as if her hypervigilance had dragged it to the surface to remind her of what she had done. But it was not only the vigilance itself that pulled the memory forward; it was the underlying conviction that she deserved this punishment, that she was fundamentally dangerous, that fed the memory its intensity and made it impossible to release. The stronger her belief that she was broken, the more the memory seemed to confirm it, arriving fully formed and sensory-rich, as if her shame was calling it up from within her. Her ex-husband had begun to notice her anxiety during their exchanges; she would flinch when he approached, and he had asked, with genuine concern, whether something else had happened. She could not tell him that she was afraid of herself.

By the time she arrived at the clinic, Layla had withdrawn almost entirely from her job. She had told her supervisor that she needed time off, but the truth was more complicated: she was afraid that her impaired judgment would hurt someone again, that she would miss something crucial in a campaign brief and cause some unforeseen harm. It was easier to stay home, to limit her contact with others, to try to make herself small and harmless. She was hoping that therapy might somehow restore her to who she had been, or at least help her understand why she had become someone she no longer recognized.
